Before I Begin, There was a time when I was full of passion. Back in college, I studied really hard. People even called me a “library ghost” because I spent so much time there. At the same time, I loved being around people, so I actively joined various gatherings and events and enjoyed connecting with others. I also started running a blog related to my field of study during college, and I continued it for about ten years. At first, I mainly wrote posts to organize and share knowledge from my major. Over time, however, my writing expanded to include my personal life, graduate school experiences, and thoughts on many different topics. Even after entering graduate school, my passion could still be seen throughout those blog posts. But as I entered the later years of my Ph.D. program, life became increasingly busy. Now that I have a child, I no longer have the same energy I once did. I also haven’t been able to write blog posts as often as before. For a long time, I told myself that it was because of the “walls of reality.” But looking back, those walls of reality were not walls at all but my “laziness”. I thought I was too busy, yet I somehow always had time to watch YouTube before going to bed. One day, I realized I was mindlessly scrolling through YouTube Shorts, moving nothing but my finger, without even knowing what I wanted to watch. At that moment, I felt deeply disappointed in myself. So, I deleted YouTube. Two days later, I installed it again. The next day, I deleted it once more. For several weeks, I repeated that cycle of deleting and reinstalling it. Then one day, a close friend I know reached out to me. He had been writing articles related to our field, and he shared how meaningful and rewarding it was to grow through writing and to encourage others to do the same. In his message, one line stood out to me: “Instead of wasting time watching dramas, entertainment shows, or YouTube videos, it is far more meaningful to spend that time studying your field and sharing that knowledge with others.” The moment I read those words, I knew. This is it. This is my chance to become someone I can respect again. I have been far too complacent. From that day on, I made up my mind. I want to return to the passionate version of myself I once knew. I want to consistently write the things I truly care about. I have not fully begun yet, but I sincerely want to thank @Photo n C a p f o r helping awaken that passion in me again. I would also like to thank @Damn a n g , who gave me a great deal of motivation. Now, I am about to begin a new journey. Five years from now, ten years from now, I hope I can become someone who inspires others in the same way.

This comes as SanDisk, which first unveiled hbftechnology, has begun building out its materials, components, and equipment supply chain. With major memory manufacturers successively launching hbfdevelopment efforts, attention is turning to whether it will generate manufacturing demand on par with HBM. According to industry sources on April 13, SanDisk has begun establishing an ecosystem with related supply chain partners to set up a pilot production line for hbfprototypes. The company plans to showcase prototypes in the second half of this year, and this is understood to involve the construction of a new pilot line. Japan is emerging as the leading candidate for the production site. A senior supply chain industry executive said, "SanDisk is in discussions with materials and equipment companies, targeting major equipment installation in H2," adding that "some companies have already begun purchase order (PO) negotiations." The industry expects the pilot line buildout to be completed in H2 with operations commencing around year-end. Commercial production is targeted for next year. hbfis a next-generation flash memory concept unveiled by SanDisk in February of last year. Its core architecture is similar to HBM. HBM, which has seen rapid growth recently as it underpins aicomputation, achieves dramatically higher speed (bandwidth) and performance by stacking DRAM. hbfinstead stacks NAND flash to increase not only bandwidth but also capacity. While hbmis a memory optimized for speed — real-time computation for aitraining — hbfmaximizes capacity. Unlike DRAM, NAND retains data without power (non-volatile), drawing attention as a new storage solution for AI. As hbfproduction infrastructure buildout accelerates, demand for process-related materials, components, and equipment is also expected to expand — signaling the emergence of an entirely new process market for manufacturing an unprecedented product. With SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics also preparing hbfalongside SanDisk, the pace of market growth could accelerate. SK Hynix is collaborating with SanDisk on hbfstandardization and other initiatives, while Samsung Electronics is independently gearing up to enter the market. Professor Kim Jung-ho of KAIST, at an hbftechnology roadmap presentation in February, projected that hbfcould surpass hbmin market size by 2038. The hbfprocess is expected to favor the existing supply chain ecosystem that has served hbmmanufacturing, given the process similarities. Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) are used to transmit signals between stacked NAND layers. The industry consensus is that companies that have established competitiveness in bonding materials and equipment (bonders) for hbmwill maintain their positions in hbfas well. An industry source stated, "Given that hbfand hbmmanufacturing do not differ significantly, there is a very high probability that the process ecosystem led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in the existing hbmmarket will carry over directly into the hbfmarket." $SNDK

[Exclusive] Samsung Foundry 2nm Yield at 55%… Stuck Below the 'Mass Production 60%' Threshold Samsung Electronics' foundry business — a key future growth engine — has hit a wall at the '60% mass production' threshold for its 2nm (nanometer; 1nm = one-billionth of a meter) process. With yields stuck in the mid-50% range and failing to enter stable mass production territory, effective yields are expected to drop to the 40% range once back-end processing is factored in. While the company has succeeded in achieving technical entry, the consensus is that it remains insufficient to win orders from global Big Tech clients. According to semiconductor industry sources on the 13th, Samsung Electronics' foundry division's average yield for the 2nm process is understood to be approximately 55%. This is lower than the '60%-plus' estimates floated by some, signaling that additional time is still needed to reach mass production stability. A source with knowledge of internal affairs stated, "The 2nm process yield is in the 50–60% range, with an average around 55%," adding, "The process is running, but it is still a long way from a stable mass production phase." The pace of yield improvement itself has been rapid. Samsung's foundry 2nm yields were reportedly stuck in the 20% range as recently as the second half of last year. Reaching the mid-50s in less than a year is assessed as technically reaching a level where the mass production line can be operated. This is attributed in part to the accumulation of process experience driven by incoming orders for Bitcoin mining chips from China's Canaan and MicroBT, among others. Given the extreme difficulty of the 2nm ultra-fine process, some consider this an exceptionally fast rate of improvement. However, the prevailing view in the industry is that it remains a "half-process" at best. In a structure where nearly half of all wafer input is discarded as defective, the process fails on both price competitiveness and delivery reliability. In particular, when factoring in losses from performance binning and packaging, the actual percentage of chips that can generate profit is estimated to fall as low as 40%. Considering that a single wafer for cutting-edge processes costs tens of millions of won, a 1% difference in yield translates to annual operating profit differences ranging from hundreds of billions to trillions of won. This is bound to significantly derail Samsung Electronics' efforts to improve foundry business profitability. An industry source said, "A yield in the 50% range only means the process 'runs' — it is not a stage where customers can entrust orders with confidence," adding, "It is a zone where both delivery and quality variability coexist." By contrast, rival TSMC is reported to have secured stable yields of 60–70% for its 2nm process. Samsung Foundry's current mid-50% yield is therefore assessed as corresponding to the technical entry stage, but falling short for securing major customers — a "transitional zone." Significant progress has been made, but analysis suggests actual mass production remains premature. In practice, Samsung has secured some customer and internal volumes, but has yet to achieve results in winning key clients such as Apple, NVIDIA, and AMD. Notably, Qualcomm — a global mobile application processor (AP) company that had raised expectations for new orders — is also showing signs of returning to TSMC, citing process yield and stability concerns. Additionally, the 'AI6' advanced autonomous driving chip contracted with Tesla is scheduled for mass production this year, and the yield level achieved at the actual production milestone will be critical in determining profitability and supply stability. Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics' strategy is to win new orders, run its facilities, and improve yields going forward. At Samsung Electronics' annual general meeting on March 18, Han Jin-man, head of the foundry business division (President), stated, "For the 2nm process as well (which is at a higher level than the 4nm process), we can build up order experience with major companies and secure yields through that process." $INTC $TSM

The optical infrastructure bubble may last longer and more persistently than expected. The market has now begun to accept this technology as essential infrastructure rather than just a trend, and from that moment on, capital is excessively concentrated in one direction. The problem is not whether this trend was wrong, but that it was correct too quickly. It is necessary to recall Cisco's past cases. At that time, Internet traffic was actually growing explosively, and there was also a clear demand for network equipment. The company grew, the industry expanded, and the direction itself was perfectly right. However, the stock price took a different path. The market reflected the future in prices too quickly, and because infrastructure always has the property of being installed ahead of demand, CAPEX was executed excessively. In the end, by the time the performance was confirmed as reality, expectations had already been exhausted, and after that, it was not a matter of growth but a collapse of valuation. The current optical infrastructure closely resembles this trend. Of course, it is difficult to explain a company like NVIDIA using the same frame. This is because they are not simple infrastructure providers but platform operators that hold the center of aicomputation and have a structure that simultaneously controls hardware, software, and the ecosystem. But the optics are different. Optics is an essential technology, but at the same time, it has a strong infrastructure nature that exists on a standardized and distributed supply chain. It is an area where substitutability exists, multiple players can enter simultaneously, and technological superiority is unlikely to lead to a long-term monopoly. In particular, the reason why optics is attracting attention now is clear. Because it is a bottleneck. Almost all problems in aiinfrastructure, including power efficiency, heat generation, data transmission distance, and signal loss, ultimately arise from interconnect, and the solutions are converging on optics. The market places the expectation that excess profits will continue in the long term for companies that resolve this bottleneck. But historically bottleneck industries always follow the same path. The moment a bottleneck is identified, capital flows in, supply expands, competition intensifies, and margins ultimately compress. What the market is seeing now is ‘demand’, and what the stock price is reflecting is the ‘complete future’. There is always a time difference between these two. Initially, expectations drive up multiples, then CAPEX expands, and at some point, supply begins to outstrip demand. From then on, even if sales increase, the stock price may actually fall. As Cisco did in the past, industry growth continues, but the return on investment follows a completely different trajectory. Another important point is that the optics industry itself is an area where it is structurally difficult to ‘secure first place.’ Technology standards are constantly changing, customers are concentrated in a few hyperscalers, and they are willing to reorganize or internalize their supply chains whenever necessary. In a structure where packaging, materials, and design are separated, it is not easy for a specific company to dominate the entire value chain. Ultimately, the assumption that No. 1 now will also be No. 1 in the future is particularly vulnerable in this industry. In the end, the key is simple. Optical infrastructure is not the wrong direction. Rather, the market is likely to grow much larger in the future. As the structure of data centers changes and aicalculations explode, optics will become a necessity, not an option. However, the problem is the expectation that the fruits of that growth will belong exclusively to a specific company, and that this expectation is already excessively reflected in the current stock price. Good industry and good investment are not the same thing. The industry may be right, but the timing may be wrong. The current optical market stands right on the borderline. Therefore, in this period, it is more important to recognize the gap between expectations and reality than to be sure of the direction.

It's not because he doesn't know, but because he knows how much time he burned to stand in that position. There is no shortcut to becoming an expert in a field. After thousands of hours of reading, tens of thousands of failures, and questions I repeat every morning, I can barely write one sentence. That one sentence has weight. However, if you look at your timeline these days, there are a lot of comments whose weight you don’t know. It is not a healthy question or opinion from a different perspective. It's about teaching experts. Armed with a YouTube video and a few blog posts, he has no hesitation in the face of an expert with 30 years of experience. In medicine, this phenomenon is especially severe. The moment a patient says “I looked it up” in the clinic, the doctor takes a moment to catch his breath. Search is good. Interest is better. However, three lines of search results cannot replace six years of medical school, several years of training, and decades of clinical experience. Healthy debate is welcome. Good questions also help experts grow. However, there is a line that should not be crossed between questioning and teaching. The line is not a matter of etiquette but of accuracy. The moment an expert's writing is overlaid with a non-expert's confidence, the reader becomes unable to distinguish which of the two is correct. And it is not the experts who suffer in the confusion, but ordinary people who need information. When I write outside of my area of ​​expertise, I always take a step back. That is not cowardice, but sincerity. Only those who know what they do not know can learn, and only those who can learn can ultimately speak properly.

Does it look different when you sit high up? ㅣ260405 1. It is no coincidence that executive offices are always located at the corners of high floors. In large corporations around the world, executives above vice president are almost without exception placed in high-rise corner offices. The place where the view is open in all directions with two or more sides of glass is not simply a large room, but is a spatial expression of the scale of thinking that the organization expects from that person. Where you sit determines how you think. 2. The view from above changes the way humans think. In psychology, research results have repeatedly emerged showing a connection between physical height and the level of abstract thinking. As you go higher, details disappear and the overall structure and flow become visible, and this visual experience naturally increases the unit of thought. It is not unrelated to this principle that people who see the big picture are ultimately able to make big decisions. 3. On the other hand, a low seat with a blocked view constricts your thoughts. Employees working in windowless office spaces tend to have high stress levels, define problems narrowly, and focus only on short-term solutions. A physically blocked space also causes psychologically blocked accidents. If the environment is narrow, your thoughts will also become narrow accordingly. 4. A view is not just a view, but a cognitive resource. In a study by the MIT Graduate School of Architecture, productivity improved by about 23% in an office environment with natural light and external views. It has been confirmed that being able to see the outside itself acts as a kind of restorative stimulus to the brain, maintaining concentration and judgment. In the end, a good view is not an aesthetic element but a functional element directly related to performance. 5. There is a long-standing organizational psychological context behind the high-rise corner office becoming a symbol of power. In American work culture, the corner office has been considered the “most important person’s seat” for decades, and people who occupy that position naturally internalize the perception that they must play a more important role. It is a structure in which space creates role expectations, and those expectations lead to actual behavior and performance. 6. High visibility leads to long-term thinking. In a study by behavioral economist Richard Fisher, the decision quality of people who think from a long-term perspective and those who only react in the short-term vary dramatically over time. The farther you look, the more likely you are to make critical decisions without being swayed by the noise in front of you. This is exactly the same principle as the physical experience of seeing widely from high up. If you go up high, you will see far away, and if you look far away, it will slowly shake. 7. Successful leaders have instinctively practiced this principle. Warren Buffett took a broad view of the entire market despite working in Omaha rather than New York's Wall Street, and Steve Jobs designed the flow of the entire experience before detail, all in the same context. They were not in a specific position, but always maintained the habit of looking furthest from the highest viewpoint. The height of vision determines the height of performance. 8. The same principle works in housing. Studies have repeatedly reported that people living in high-rise residential spaces with secured views have higher psychological stability and self-efficacy than those living in environments without such views. Seeing a wide-open landscape without feeling stuffy every morning has an impact on determining the size of your thoughts for the day. The quality of life and thinking are connected to the quality of what we see. 9. In the end, “where you live is important” is not about real estate. The scale of a person is created by accumulating the perspective with which he or she starts the day, works, and thinks every day. A low, narrow, and closed environment makes thinking low, narrow, and closed, and a high, wide, and open environment has the opposite effect. The environment is a quiet variable that sets the upper limit of thinking. 10. If you cannot sit in a corner office on a high floor right now, the next step is to raise the altitude of your thoughts first. The starting point is to train your perspective to look down on any problem from one level above and intentionally expand the landscape you see. It's not that people who sit high up think differently, but those who practice thinking differently first eventually get there. The view is the starting point, not the destination.

text: It seems like Google has sharpened its sword... 🫨 They have applied for a patent aimed at reducing the memory dependence of the llmmodel. [0009] This technique reduces the transmission of model parameters in multiple layers and reduces the transmission of attention cache data in the attention layer, thereby reducing overall processing latency. The system achieves these benefits without having to allocate additional extremely limited on-chip memory to store model weights or attention cache data. These techniques do not require larger on-chip memory (e.g., memory in the processor or accelerator) and do not increase the on-chip memory allocation. [0010] The system can reduce the amount of on-chip memory required or the amount of on-chip memory used. As explained in more detail below, the system can perform the step of predicting the top k weights or tokens using an approximation matrix that has a smaller data size or memory storage size than the full matrix of the neural network. In some implementations, the approximation matrix for each layer of the neural network can be trained or adjusted to predict the top k elements of that layer to a predetermined level of accuracy, often during the neural network training process. Once training is complete, the approximation matrix for the layer can be stored along with the overall weights or parameters and used during inference. The size of the approximation matrix can be made smaller, for example, by storing parameter values ​​for a smaller number of parameters (e.g. using a low-order approximation matrix) or by quantizing the parameter values ​​to reduce the number of bits required for each parameter value. As a result, loading an approximation matrix requires less data to be transferred to the on-chip memory of an accelerator or other processor than transferring the original matrix. Once the weight subset (including the top k weights) is determined, the system can load only a portion of the weights from the original matrix for that layer. Instead of sending the entire matrix, the system can load and process only selected parts of the matrix (for example, load and process only the weights contained in a subset, or load and process only a specific group of weights that contains the weights contained in the subset). Therefore, the maximum on-chip memory capacity required to process a neural network layer can be reduced because the approximation matrix and the selected portion of the full matrix used in a given processing cycle are smaller than the data size of the full matrix.

Thank you for your thoughtful writing!

As soon as quantum sensing starts to make money, the biggest obstacle will be how to turn those fragile quantum states into practical machines. Existing quantum systems were packed with lasers, mirrors, and control devices on an optical table. It was large, consumed a lot of power, and had a structure where signals were damaged by vibration or temperature changes. This SWAP (Size, Weight, And Power) bottleneck was the real wall blocking the commercialization of quantum sensing. The solution that Infleqtion focuses on is ‘Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC)’. It is a method of integrating a laser array, miniature frequency comb, and spatial light modulator into one chip using silicon photonics technology. Through this, we aim to reduce size, weight, power, and cost (C-SWaP) by 10 to up to 10,000 times. Just looking at the Tiqker optical atomic clock roadmap, this direction is clear. Starting from the current 3U rack size, it is expected to expand to data centers, aiclusters, and defense and space fields as it undergoes picintegration and is compressed to ≤3U and even <0.5L. We are already verifying picosecond-level precise timing in the field in White Rabbit integration with Safran, Royal Navy submarine demonstration, and Quantum Corridor network testing. Added to this is ‘AI-based quantum control.’ Like Q-CTRL or Infleqtion's Contextual Machine Learning (CML), the software compensates for noise and suppresses decoherence in real time. It is a strategy to compensate for the physical vulnerabilities of hardware with software. As a result, inertial navigation in GPS-denied environments and ultra-high sensitivity magnetic field and gravity measurements can operate reliably even on actual moving platforms (submarines, drones, vehicles). The strengths of the neutral atom platform shine even brighter here. As sensing (Tiqker, inertial sensor) and computing (Sqale) share the same hardware stack, the picminiaturization effect can be applied to both at the same time. Unlike nvcenters or other solid-state sensors, rubidium-based neutral atoms are relatively advantageous for precise control even near room temperature, and the possibility of mass production using meta-surfaces is high. Of course, complete chip-scale integration is still in progress. Remaining challenges include manufacturing yield, cost optimization, and long-term stability in extreme environments (vibration and magnetic fields). However, looking at Infleqtion's financial update for 2025-2026 and demonstrations from CES 2026, there are strong signs that these technology variables are quickly becoming a reality. In the end, the real game changer in quantum sensing is not “how to turn the weaknesses of the quantum state into strengths,” but how quickly the combination of picminiaturization + aicontrol reaches the level of practical deployment. The most exciting point right now is that Infleqtion is pushing both axes simultaneously with its neutral atom single platform.

text: Scale-Up is the approach of connecting accelerators more tightly within a single compute domain. Inside a single rack, GPUs or XPUs are bound together through a unified memory-semantic fabric so they operate as one massive compute engine. NVIDIA’s NVLink is the canonical example. Connection distances range from meters to tens of meters, and copper (AEC, Active Electrical Cable) can physically handle these distances.[5] Scale-Out is the stage of connecting rack to rack within a data center. InfiniBand and Ethernet are the primary protocols, and distances extend from tens to hundreds of meters. Copper can’t keep up, and PAM4-based optical transceivers (400G, 800G, 1.6T) become essential. This is precisely why CPO (Co-Packaged Optics) switches are gaining traction.[5] Scale-Across is data center to data center, campus to campus, region to region connectivity. Distances stretch from 2 km to thousands of kilometers. Without coherent ZR/ZR+ technology, this is simply not possible. As aimodels begin exceeding the power limits and physical space of a single data center, demand at this layer is growing rapidly.[6]

1. Why do I need to take the laser out? • Hellish heat: aiaccelerators (GPU, etc.) are extremely hot (over 500W). If the laser is placed right next to it, the laser will easily break down due to heat and its lifespan will be shortened. • Limitations in maintenance: If the laser breaks down, the entire expensive switch or accelerator cannot be removed. Only the laser must be able to be easily replaced from the outside. • Solution (ELS): So, the laser is placed on the cool outside (faceplate), and the method of sending only light through optical fibers to the 'optical engine' on the inside (external laser, ELS) is becoming a trend. 2. The market is growing with standardization. • In the past, specifications were different for each company, so only customized products were produced. • Now, OIF (Optical Internet Forum) has established a common standard called ELSFP. As manufacturing becomes easier, mass production and replacement of parts becomes easier. • The market will grow in earnest from 2027, so the company that finalizes the design and passes the quality test now (2026) will be the winner. 3. POET Technologies' Weapon • Problems with the existing method: Assembling existing optical components uses the 'active alignment' method, in which people or equipment precisely adjust the positions of the lens and laser one by one, making mass production difficult and expensive. • POET's cheat key (Optical) Interposer): Just like making semiconductors, all guides are dug in advance at the wafer level. Therefore, 'passive alignment' is possible by simply placing a laser chip on it. • Result: Claimed that assembly costs can be reduced by up to 75% compared to existing methods.

NVIDIA announces strategic partnership investing $2 billion (approximately 2.8 trillion won) in Marvell So, we need to look back at Marvell's OFC 2026 one more time. Marvell acquired Photonic Fabric™ when it closed its acquisition of Celestial aiin February 2026. And at OFC 2026, this technology was fully deployed as the core of multi-rack optical scale-up. If you look at this point, it may seem like “strengthening optical connections.” However, the moment NVIDIA investment is added, the interpretation changes. Marvell is no longer just an optical components company. Within the AI ​​factory ecosystem cultivated by NVIDIA, it has been upgraded to a strategic partner that can handle custom XPU, NVLink Fusion compatible scale-up networking, and silicon photonics. In other words, Marvell's Photonic Fabric™ is not a “good technology,” but has become a scale-up optical interconnect card that NVIDIA directly recognized as necessary. What is important is the direction. The AI ​​infrastructure bottleneck is no longer simply a matter of the number of GPUs, but a matter of how fast and low-power the connection between GPUs and racks is. NVIDIA is trying to expand that section with its NVLink ecosystem, and Marvell is filling the void with Celestial AI's Photonic Fabric™. In other words, this investment is not a simple financial investment, but is closer to a move to incorporate optical-based scale-up into the NVIDIA standard ecosystem. The acquisition of Celestial aisecured optical scale-up technology, and the investment in NVIDIA raised the possibility of adoption of the technology and its ecosystem status. What this combination means is clear. In the future, it is highly likely that aidata centers will not only scale-out to optical, but also scale-up to optical. And Marvell has emerged as one of the key vendors in that transition. The fact that NVIDIA invested $2 billion is a sign that this game can grow much faster than expected. So, we have to look back at Marvell OFC 2026 one more time. If Celestial aitechnology is responsible for scale-up, the technologies below played a role in complementing/expanding it. • 1.6T Optical DSP (Ara T / Ara • Lumentum and Live OCS (Optical Circuit Switching) demo: Aquila 1.6T + Ara 1.6T + COLORZ 800Z and Lumentum R300 OCS → Rack-level live demo that dynamically connects multi-rack scale-up of Photonic Fabric. • Structera S 60260 (260-lane PCIe 6.0 Switch) & Structera S 30260 (CXL Switch): Enhanced GPU/memory pooling within scale-up → Completely resolves memory wall with Photonic Fabric. • RELIANT™ telemetry platform: Real-time monitoring/optimization of entire optical fabric (including photonic fabric). Overall, we emphasized a portfolio that covers aiscale-up/out/across all at once, and Photonic Fabric™ has established itself as a “game changer” in scale-up. Ultimately, this elaborately crafted Marvell technology is expected to become one of the pillars of NVIDIA, and monetization is expected to begin in earnest in the second half of FY2028.

This is about why they sit in an interesting structural position as silicon photonics scales.$forM(FormFactor) — Every picwafer needs to be characterized before it gets diced. Process variation in silicon photonics is brutal; small deviations in waveguide geometry or grating etch show up immediately as insertion loss or yield failure. FormFactor's CM300 is the tool that enables optical wafer-level probing — coupling light directly to the wafer to test photonic performance in situ, before any packaging happens. More silicon photonics wafer starts across TSMC, GFS, and ifsmeans more demand for that capability, regardless of who wins the chip design race.$AEHR(Aehr Test Systems) — Silicon photonics devices go into hyperscale data centers running 24/7. Burn-in testing is how you screen out infant mortality before the device ships. Aehr has built wafer-level burn-in systems specifically suited for compound semiconductor and photonic devices. As reliability standards for optical interconnects tighten, this becomes less optional.$KEYS(Keysight) — You cannot characterize a 200G or 400G photonic device without instrumentation that can actually keep up with it. Keysight's optical and rftest equipment sits at every serious piccharacterization bench, in both R&D and production. As data rates climb, older test infrastructure gets retired and replaced. Keysight benefits from both ends — new technology development and the production ramp that follows.

Reference[59] in the TurboQuant paper And I will share what was said in this paper and by field gurus. (I have also posted a few posts related to this since last year. Last year, a major memory researcher in China was KV Cache...) ———- 1. kvcache compression is not an issue that came out of nowhere, but a growing trend that has already been building up. The recent debate surrounding the memory industry seems to have changed the game with the emergence of a certain technology, but in reality, that is not the case. Methods for reducing or handling kvcache have been studied for a long time, and there is not just one method. Attempts have continued to reduce the computational burden by expressing data with fewer bits, removing less important parts, grouping similar information, or changing the structure itself. What has changed recently is that there is a shift from the attitude of “let’s keep the original version as much as possible” to “it is okay to reduce it more drastically as long as the core meaning is maintained.” As agent-type aiincreases, it is no longer simply a matter of reducing a chunk of cache, but an important issue is how to handle the entire task state and context that comes and goes in the intermediate inference stage more lightly and efficiently. In other words, rather than an improvement in storage technology, it is more correct to view it as a trend that changes the way aicarries on thinking itself to be more efficient. 2. Even if compression technology develops, memory demand is likely to increase rather than decrease. On the surface, compressing the cache appears to reduce memory use. But real markets don't work that simple. As costs go down, companies and services will not only do existing tasks more cheaply, but will also try longer context processing, more complex question and answering, more concurrent users, and more agent integrations that were previously considered too burdensome. This is similar to the phenomenon that widening the road does not make car movement easier, but rather causes more cars to gather. The same goes for aiservices now. Features such as long-winded reasoning, multiple consecutive conversations, multi-agent operations, and maintaining session state still require a lot of memory. Therefore, efficiency technology is closer to a technology that opens up uses that have been closed due to cost, rather than a technology that eliminates memory demand. In the end, the key is not how much less memory is used on a single server, but how much larger the overall service scale and inference volume can be. 3. The real problem is not the importance of memory, but that memory companies are still lagging behind. Memory is still a very important component of aiinfrastructure. However, the fact that it is an important component and the fact that it is leading the market are different. In fact, much of the high added value is already moving to higher-level areas such as computational chips such as GPUs and NPUs, packaging, interconnects, controllers, and system software. hbmis also an example of this trend. Memory itself is essential, but money and influence are generated not from individual memories, but from how they are tied to the entire system. However, the memory industry is still accustomed to large-scale facility investments, long development cycles, and standards-centered thinking. Simply put, the method is, “When the market grows sufficiently and the requirements become clear, we will supply accordingly.” The problem is that the AI ​​market does not wait that long. Service companies or model developers are busy running and optimizing models within a given hardware environment, and do not design new memory structures on their behalf. Therefore, in the future, memory companies should more actively explain which memory structures are advantageous for which aitasks, what speed and capacity configurations are necessary, and why such structures are meaningful in the market. The biggest reason why the memory semiconductor fab operates at 100% is due to process characteristics. Therefore, to be more precise, rather than continuing to operate due to fixed costs, the best option is to operate at 100% because the fixed costs are inevitably high due to the special nature of the semiconductor process. To produce memory, hundreds of steps, including major processes such as exposure, etching, and deposition, must be continuously interconnected. In this situation, if the line is stopped even for a moment, the entire process must be inspected when restarted, so it takes several months to reestablish the yield, and if the clean room environment is reset, time and cost increase explosively. In addition, since certain equipment must maintain high temperature/high vacuum conditions at all times, turning it off even for a short period of time can cause greater damage, both from the yield point of view as mentioned above. In other words, it is difficult to physically stop the process due to the nature of the process. Even if some factories stop or reduce production, fixed costs such as depreciation, labor, and clean room maintenance remain the same, so even if you are losing money due to memory prices, continuing production without stopping will inevitably reduce losses even a little compared to not producing. Due to the nature of the process, the burden of fixed costs increases, which is why the factory must continue to operate even if it is at a deficit. That is why memory companies such as Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron are considering expansion. Demand appears to be good, so once capacity is expanded, production cannot be reduced. In this way, if demand forecasting fails, excess inventory becomes a factor, and excess inventory becomes a factor in reducing memory prices. Because of these factors, memory semiconductors are classified as commodities.

Formfactor company appears in this article, but since it is only a brief technical explanation, I will write about FormFactor company's Pharos Probe Series in more detail. The Pharos Probe Series (especially the Pharos Edge Short Lens / Long Lens versions) is an optical probe developed to directly test silicon photonics (SiPh) chips in the wafer state. This is a technology that allows the entire wafer to be inspected without the need to dice the chips and make them into individual dies as in the existing method. The key is an ultra-precision 3D-printed micro-lens (Pharos lens) made with 'two-photon lithography'. This lens adopts a periscope structure to efficiently bend the vertical light coming down from the optical fiber 90 degrees horizontally and accurately inject (couple) it into the edge (side) waveguide of the chip. <1. ‘Nano-precision 3D printing’ technology made with two-photon lithography> This technology is on a different level from regular 3D printers. Think of it as ultra-precision micro-sculpture, where a laser pen is used to “draw” point by point into liquid resin and harden it. Because the laser hardens the resin only by absorbing two photons simultaneously, the reaction occurs only in an extremely small volume (nanometer level) that is in focus. So you can freely create 3D shapes in air or liquid. While traditional lenses are made by glass grinding or injection molding, Pharos lenses 3D print complex freeform optical structures in one step at nanometer resolution. Result: Even though it is ultra-small (micrometer size), optical loss is extremely low, and the custom Mode Field Diameter (MFD, the size at which light spreads) can be precisely matched to the waveguide. Light efficiency is maximized, as if “fitting the pipe diameter to prevent water leakage.” This makes the lens extremely small, light and precise, allowing it to easily fit into narrow trenches or V-grooves on the wafer. <2. Periscope structure — the magic of ‘smartly’ bending vertical light horizontally> Optical fibers usually send light vertically down from above. However, the waveguide of a silicon photonics chip is located on the side (edge) of the chip, so light must be input horizontally to work properly. It's just like a submarine periscope! The submarine is hidden underwater, but we use the periscope mirror to ‘see’ the ocean above horizontally, then turn 90 degrees to look inside the submarine. The Pharos lens also uses 3D printing to create a periscope structure, such as a micro-mirror or prism, inside the lens, which bends vertically incident light exactly 90 degrees to create a horizontal beam and shoots it to the edge of the chip. Thanks to this structure, the coupling loss is very low at less than 1.5 dB (maximum 1.51 dB/facet) and there is almost no polarization dependence. Existing tapered lensed fibers had to be aligned manually, and they were difficult to use in production because they easily damaged chips or had large alignment errors. Pharos lenses feature self-alignment + patented fiducial (optical reference points) that enable automatic calibration at the nanometer level. <3. Pharos Edge Short Lens vs Long Lens — ‘Customized’ version optimized for V-groove / Trench > Silicon wafers are pre-etched with a trench (rectangular groove) or V-groove (V-shaped groove) for edge coupling. Short Lens: Optimized for shorter trench depth and short working distance. Quickly tests by fitting into a narrow, shallow groove. Long Lens: Optimized for deeper V-groove and long working distance. The V-shaped groove is deep, so the lens is designed to be long so that light can be accurately injected from a greater distance. Additional Vertical version: for grating coupler (surface grating coupler), also supports vertical coupling. Just as the vehicle type (short/long lens) is selected depending on whether the car parking lot entrance is narrow, straight (trench) or slanted, V-shaped (V-groove), the optimal lens is selected according to the shape and depth of the groove to achieve the highest efficiency. <4. So why is this technology innovative? > (1) Wafer-level full automated testing Thousands of measurements can be made on one wafer. The existing lab method took several days to several months due to manual + dicing post-testing, but Pharos is capable of testing within 5 seconds per die, repeatability within 0.2 dB, and long-term stability at the level of 0.01 dB. (2) Productivity explosion SiPh chips such as data centers, aiaccelerators, LiDAR, 5G optical transceivers, and quantum optical devices can be tested immediately at the mass production stage, greatly shortening the time-to-yield. (3) Full integration with FormFactor system interconnection CM300xi-SiPh probe station + Velox software + AutoCal (automatic calibration). It is designed so that even beginners can use it easily.

In some ways, TurboQuant is a panic cell behind the development of good technology, which led to a plunge in memory prices. Do you really feel that memory demand will decrease? You can first solve the genius quiz that I posted as a comment in another post, and then come back to this post. It seems more appropriate to view kvcache, which is mentioned as a major application of TurboQuant, not as "external long-term storage memory" (gpumemory itself, such as hbmor DDR), but as "working memory" that is maintained in real time during inference (running time). As a temporary cache memory that continues to store the Key and Value of previous tokens when the model processes conversations or long contexts. Why is this important? Previously, as the context length became longer, the kvcache consumed gpumemory exponentially. (sometimes up to 80-90% of inference memory) TurboQuant compresses this kvcache by ~6x (3-bit level) without loss of accuracy, while speeding up attention operations by up to 8x. (Based on H100) As a result, what can be done with the same hardware increases significantly as follows: 1. Context length significantly increases → Contexts that are 4 to 6 times (or more) longer can be processed with the same memory. Significant improvements in long document summaries, codebase-wide analysis, very long multi-turn conversations, and Agentic AI, where agents remember multiple steps. 2. Increased concurrent user/batch size → More requests can be processed simultaneously with the same server → Service capacity increased by nearly 6 times (since memory bottleneck is resolved). 3. Cost efficiency → You can do more with the same gpuor achieve similar performance with a cheaper GPU. Did you answer the quiz attached to the image? I believe that answer number 2 (“Fill all 6 slots and receive 6 times more services/subscribers”) is a much more realistic and aggressive strategy. Like number 1, “buy only one memory and save money” is only a short-term cost saving, but is likely to be a missed opportunity in the long run, and is also not a correct understanding when looking at the actual location of the kvcache. These efficiency gains (similar to the Jevons paradox) may appear to reduce memory demand in the short term, but in the long term, as aiservices become cheaper and more powerful, they are likely to explode overall demand (longer contexts, more usage). The same article came out saying that memory usage would be reduced to 1/6, but I shouted “a big hit” and the market shouted “a crash.” If it develops in a healthy direction, we expect that it will be an opportunity for expansion of aibase and increase in memory demand, rather than a decrease in memory demand.

In the era of space solar power, talk about perovskite tandem batteries is slowly emerging. Hanwha Solutions, which recently increased its paid-in capital, also announced that it would pay off its debt and invest the remainder in perovskite. 1. Perovskite is a structure name, not a substance name. It is an ABX3 structured material that is easier to make using a solution-base process than existing polysilicon solar cells, but has higher efficiency. And because it can be made in a thin film form, it can be made much smaller than before. 2. Combine this with existing polysilicon solar cells and combine two types of solar cells on the front and back. The reason for this is that the two materials have different band gaps, so the light ranges used are different. Perovskites that use the ultraviolet to visible light range with short wavelengths are placed on the top, which receives light, and solar cells that use visible and infrared rays are placed on the bottom. This allows more wavelengths of light to be used than before, dramatically increasing efficiency. 3. In order to be commercialized, it must be grown in a large area on a laboratory cell scale (Gate 1), check whether the cells grown in a large area can withstand humidity and uvstress under international standard conditions (Gate 2), prepare for mass production by securing a manufacturing scale from mwto GW (Gate 3), and go through the process of commercialization (Gate 4) where it is actually released to the market and guaranteed by insurance companies. Currently, Hanwha Solutions is in the Gate 2 process where reliability has been secured and is not yet ready for mass production, but it looks like it will move to the Gate 3 stage with large investments. Professor Chenming Hu was born in Taiwan, completed his master's and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering at UC Berkeley, went on to MIT, and served as a professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at UC Berkeley. These innovations in theory, model, and device structure have played a key role in simultaneously improving semiconductor performance, power, and integration by enabling ‘practical transistors that operate even at the nanoscale.’ Additionally, he served as the first Cto (Chief Technology Officer) of TSMC, the world's largest foundry company, in the early 2000s and played a decisive role in connecting device and process ideas from the lab with the mass production roadmap. Does anyone know this story? I would like to briefly talk about the SOI wafer story/patent war. Many people think that SOI wafers are only used for rfchips, or some may think they are only used for SiPh, but in fact, they are a core substrate for silicon photonics that connects aidata centers today, and are also used for rfchips. In the late 1990s, Professor Chen Ming-Hu of UC Berkeley invented Finfeton an SOI substrate, but there is a story that SOI problems made it unsuitable for mass production, such as being too expensive, floating body effect, increased leakage current, and poor heat conduction. Professor Jong-ho Lee (former Minister) solved this problem. While working at Wonkwang University, in collaboration with KAisT, he developed a structure that connects pins directly to the bulk silicon substrate instead of SOI. It solved thermal/electrical problems at the same time and opened the way to mass production with cheap wafers. Instead of SOI, US Patent Application: February 4, 2003, Intel filed ten days later. Samsung and TSMC in 2004. Intel paid a license fee of about 10 billion won in 2012, but Samsung refused: even though it requested joint research with Professor Lee and lectures before mass production. The SOI Wafer You Didn't Know About — And the Patent War It Started Not many people know that SOI wafers aren't just for RF chips. They're also the backbone of silicon photonics — the technology wiring up AI datacenters right now. But here's a story most people outside Korea have never heard. In the late 1990s, UC Berkeley's Chenming Hu invented the FinFET on SOI wafers. Problem: SOI is expensive, suffers from floating body effects, poor thermal conductivity, and increased leakage. Fine for research, not for mass production. A Korean professor named Jong-Ho Lee (이종호) solved this. Working at Wonkwang University with KAIST, he built the FinFET on bulk silicon instead — fins connected directly to the substrate. Thermal and electrical problems solved. Cheap wafers. Manufacturable at scale. He filed the U.S. patent on February 4, 2003. Intel filed theirs ten days later. Samsung and TSMC didn't file until 2004. Intel paid ~$10 M in licensing fees in 2012. Samsung refused — despite having collaborated with Prof. Lee and even calling him back to lecture their engineers before mass production. In 2016, KAIST's subsidiary sued Samsung in the Eastern District of Texas. Samsung tried everything: reporting Prof. Lee for unauthorized tech export, filing for patent invalidation (denied), pressuring his former university to claim ownership. None of it worked.$400 M. 2020: court judgment at $200 M. Samsung settled for an undisclosed amount.$13 M in deposits — "mostly from patent income."

Drawing from my experience working at AMD AECG until last year, let me add some technical commentary on this. Once a satellite is launched, that's it. No one can go up and swap out a chip. But mission requirements keep changing. Communication protocols get updated, sensor algorithms improve, and unexpected situations arise. ASICs have their logic baked in, so no changes are possible after launch. CPUs are flexible but slow. FPGAs deliver hardware-level speed while allowing you to remotely reprogram the logic itself from orbit. It's the only chip you can fix in an environment where nothing can be fixed. The company that made FPGAs better than anyone was Xilinx. Across space, defense, telecom, and data centers, Xilinx was the undisputed number one in FPGAs. amdacquired the company for roughly $50 billion in 2022. For AMD, this meant securing an entirely new pillar, Programmable Logic, on top of CPUs and GPUs.$amdholds two seats at the table in space data centers. There is a shift in quantum computing strategy at Google. They say they will only pursue the existing superconducting qubits and will also adopt the neutral atom method at the same time. It is expressed as any to any connectivity, and it appears to be an attempt to compensate for the scalability limitations of superconducting qubits with the characteristic that many neutral atoms can be flexibly connected at once. In optical connection, the neutral atom qubit can be used as a repeater or memory to adjust timing. However, even if the limitations of scale-up are overcome, neutral atoms have great difficulty in stably executing deep circuits with many cycles, so another break-through appears to be necessary. The 25-year neutral atom method had a qecround of 4.45ms in the surface code experiment. In deep-circuit, the logical teleportation layer was 41.9ms, and it is claimed that it can go to the 4ms level when optimized, which is the SOTA level. In other words, one error correction should take at least several ms. On the other hand, superconductivity only takes about 1.1us based on the Google Willow chip. Isn't the error correction speed of Zhongseo atom too slow just for the currently reported cycle time? This error correction is frequently performed in the middle of calculation, creating a significant bottleneck in calculation speed. Coherence time may be used up while waiting for error correction. So, it seems that there is a task to solve this problem at the system level. I am looking forward to seeing how well they will solve the neutral atom problem, which is the second key axis.

As of 2026, silicon photonics and CPO (Co-Packaged Optics) have completely moved beyond the stage of simple new technologies and have become the actual core foundation of aidata center infrastructure. At a time when aiclusters require node bandwidths of more than 100Tb/s, the existing copper-based electrical signaling method has reached physical limitations, and only light-based transmission methods can fundamentally solve this bottleneck. 2. The key trigger for this transition is the “Copper Wall”. Because high-speed electrical signals begin to deteriorate when transmitted more than about 1 meter, aiclusters were confined to single racks or small rows. On the other hand, silicon photonics can transmit over 100 meters without signal loss, making it a reality to bundle an aifactory with a scale of 'one million GPUs' into one logical resource. 3. cpois a structure that drastically shortens the electrical path by integrating the switch ASIC and optical engine in the same package. This relaxes signal equalization requirements and simultaneously reduces power consumption and latency. It has an overwhelming advantage in both energy efficiency and bandwidth compared to the traditional pluggable optical module method. 4. TSMC's COUPE (Compact Universal Photonic Engine) platform is currently in the final mass production verification stage and is scheduled for full-scale mass production in the second half of 2026. Both NVIDIA and Broadcom are building their own cposolutions based on this platform and SoIC-X 3D packaging technology. Submillimeter-level interconnect distances are realized by stacking 65nm optical integrated circuits (PICs) directly on electronic ICs. 5. NVIDIA and Broadcom have different strategic directions. NVIDIA is combining NVLink and cpoto build a vertically integrated performance fortress within its aiecosystem, while Broadcom is taking a strategy to leverage its existing installed base by spreading cpoas an open industry standard across Ethernet networks. The competition between the two giants is structured to further speed up the entire cpoecosystem. 6. STMicroelectronics officially began mass production of silicon photonics for aidata centers in March 2026 and announced plans to more than quadruple production by 2027. Tower Semiconductor has officially confirmed its plan to triple its SiPh production capacity by mid-2026. This is not just a development phase, but a physical investment based on long-term capacity reservations from actual hyperscaler customers. 7. Technology trends in the silicon photonics market in 2026 are largely summarized into four categories. The first is the advancement of optical module speed from 1.6T to 3.2T, the second is heterogeneous integration of SiPh + TFLN (thin film lithium niobate) / III-V platform, the third is the expansion of optical interconnects to replace copper inside aisystems, and the fourth is the emergence of the 'optical chiplet' marketplace through UCIe-S/UCIe-A standardization. 8. From a supply chain perspective, the benefits of this flow are distributed throughout the broader value chain. Starting from substrate materials ($AXTI's indium substrate, $IQE's compound semiconductor epiwafer), the ecosystem extends to optical transceiver manufacturing ($AAOI, $LITE, $COHR), test and measurement ($KEYS, $VIAV, $forM), optical fiber infrastructure ($GLW, Fujikura, Sumitomo), and foundry and packaging ($TSM, $TSEM, $UMC). It is a structure in which all layers grow simultaneously. $IQE (+282.5%), $AXTI (+246.6%), $AAOI (+157.37%), $SIVE (+113.08%), $SOI (+103.54%), and $LITE (+100.27%) all serve as key bottlenecks in the expansion of aioptical infrastructure. "Jensen Huang recently sat down with Joe Rogan for a wide-ranging two-hour conversation about computing, AI, and the future of technology (jreepisode #2422, Dec 3, 2025). Jensen is one of the clearest thinkers in tech, and he has a gift for making complex ideas accessible. As someone working in quantum computing, I found myself taking notes throughout. Much of what Jensen said resonated. Some of it prompted me to think about where quantum computing fits into this picture. 1. The Platform That Made AI Possible One of Jensen's most compelling explanations in the podcast was about CUDA; Not as a product, but as a paradigm shift. He described how NVIDIA realized that their graphics chips, designed for rendering pixels in parallel, could be reprogrammed for general-purpose computation. The hardware mattered, but CUDA is what turned it into a general-purpose computing platform that developers could build on. He’s right, and it’s a lesson that applies across computing. The companies that shape industries are often the ones that make powerful hardware accessible, repeatable, and scalable through software, tooling, and an ecosystem. Quantum is earlier in that journey, but the same logic holds. CUDA-Q is a serious attempt at a unified programming model for hybrid quantum-classical workflows that can target different qpubackends. QuEra's systems integrate with CUDA-Q, and we think that kind of orchestration layer matters if quantum is going to slot into real hpcand aienvironments rather than remain a bespoke lab exercise. What I’d add is this: GPUs and quantum computers are not interchangeable forms of parallelism. GPUs shine when you can apply similar operations across massive datasets. Quantum targets a different class of problems, where the structure of the computation can create interference effects that classical parallelism cannot exploit. The future likely involves both, working together in hybrid workflows. For teams evaluating quantum: The CUDA lesson is simple: integration friction determines adoption. Ask whether a quantum platform gives your developers a productive way to iterate, including emulation, debugging, and workflow integration. The hardware matters, but the software determines whether you can actually use it. 2. The "Universal Function Approximator" Jensen offered what I think is the most elegant explanation of deep learning I've heard: neural networks are "universal function approximators." Given enough examples of inputs and outputs, a sufficiently large network can learn the mapping between them, essentially learning any function you can provide training data for. He went further, specifically mentioning physics. If you can generate enough examples of how physical systems behave, including systems governed by quantum mechanics like Schrödinger's equation, neural networks can learn to approximate those physics. This is already happening: aimodels trained on physical simulations are now making predictions about molecular behavior, materials properties, and more. Jensen’s universal function approximator needs teachers. For many physics problems, the teacher is classical simulation or experimental data. But in regimes where quantum effects dominate, generating reliable training data can become the bottleneck. Classical methods can get expensive fast as system complexity grows, and in some domains the approximations you make to keep costs reasonable are exactly what you wish you didn’t have to assume. This is where I see quantum fitting into Jensen’s vision, not as a competitor to aibut as a new source of high-value data and validation. A quantum computer can generate samples and observables from quantum processes that are difficult to reproduce classically at scale. Those outputs can be used to train or calibrate surrogate models, and just as importantly, to stress-test them in the regimes where you most need confidence. We’re already seeing early versions of this workflow. Partners using our neutral-atom systems generate quantum state distributions and measurements that feed into classical machine learning models. The quantum hardware does what it’s uniquely good at, producing structured quantum data, while classical aidoes what it’s good at, learning compact representations and running fast inference. For teams building AI-for-physics pipelines: The opportunity is to treat quantum as an additional instrument in your modeling workflow. Where can quantum generate or validate data in regimes that are hard to reach classically? Where can it stress-test your surrogate models? The hybrid loop between classical learning and physics-grounded quantum evaluation is where the practical value lies. 3. Quantum and Encryption When quantum computing came up in the conversation, it was primarily in the context of cybersecurity. Jensen explained that quantum computers could potentially break current encryption methods, and that "the entire industry is working" on post-quantum cryptography: new encryption standards that will be secure against both classical and quantum attacks. This is all accurate. NisT has finalized its first post-quantum cryptography standards. Migration timelines are being set across government and industry. It's a real and urgent priority that responsible organizations are taking seriously. But I'd offer a somewhat different lens on what quantum computing actually represents. Cryptographically relevant quantum computers, the kind that could break rsaor elliptic curve cryptography, require millions of physical qubits with error rates far below what any platform has demonstrated today. Even optimistic projections put this capability a decade or more away. It's important to prepare for, which is why the cryptography migration is happening now, but it's not imminent. Meanwhile, systems with hundreds of qubits exist today, and hardware quality is improving steadily. These machines can already tackle meaningful problems in optimization, simulation, and sampling. These are problems with commercial relevance right now, not in some distant future. The framing of quantum primarily as a threat to encryption, while technically accurate in the long term, reminds me of how GPUs might have been described in 1999 if someone had focused only on their eventual potential to make current video games obsolete. True, but you'd miss the revolution that was actually unfolding in parallel computing, scientific visualization, and eventually AI. Quantum computing's near-term value isn't about breaking things. It's about building things: simulating molecular interactions for drug discovery, optimizing logistics networks, solving combinatorial problems that bottleneck classical systems. For teams navigating security constraints: The encryption narrative, while narrow, does shape real buying decisions. Security posture determines where you can run workloads, what data you can move, and which procurement paths are viable. Many government and regulated buyers cannot place sensitive workloads in public clouds; they require on-premises deployment for sovereignty, compliance, and ipprotection. That's why the market is segmenting: cloud access for broad experimentation, on-premises options for sovereignty-driven deployments. Understand which category your workloads fall into. 4. Energy as the Binding Constraint One of Jensen's most striking arguments was about energy. He made the case that energy availability is the fundamental constraint on aigrowth, and on industrial growth more broadly. "Without energy growth, we can have no industrial growth," he said. He predicted that aidatacenters would eventually be co-located with small modular nuclear reactors, and he emphasized that accelerated computing has improved performance per watt by orders of magnitude, making aiworkloads far more energy-efficient than running them on general-purpose CPUs. I found this compelling, and it connects to something that doesn't get enough attention in quantum computing: the energy footprint of different qubit technologies. Superconducting quantum computers, the kind ibmoperates, require dilution refrigerators that maintain temperatures near absolute zero (around 15 millikelvin, colder than outer space). Cryogenic infrastructure adds significant facility complexity and overhead. As systems scale to more qubits, these requirements grow. Neutral-atom systems like the ones QuEra builds work differently. The quantum operations happen in an ultra-high vacuum chamber, but the external environment is room temperature. QuEra uses lasers and precision optics rather than millikelvin refrigeration. The engineering challenges are different, not absent. Every quantum platform has hard problems to solve, but the cooling requirements are fundamentally different in kind. I don't want to overclaim here. But as datacenters become increasingly energy-constrained, and as Jensen's vision of GPU-dense aifactories pushes power budgets to their limits, the incremental energy cost of adding quantum acceleration matters. A quantum system that integrates into an hpccenter without requiring dedicated cryogenic infrastructure has real operational advantages. For teams planning facility integration: The honest question to ask is not "how many qubits," but "what is the energy and cost required to reach a validated result?" How does the system fit into your facility and operational model? What hybrid workflow delivers measurable improvement in time-to-answer or cost-to-answer for your target problems? And critically: what's the path from today's experiments to tomorrow's scaled capability? 5. Diffusion, Not a Single Moment One of the most valuable parts of Jensen’s conversation was his description of how transformative technologies actually spread. He pushed back on the idea of a single “agimoment” where everything changes overnight. Instead, he described progress as diffusion: capability seeps into products, workflows, and institutions over time, and the impact compounds. He used the analogy of cars: engines became more powerful over time, but that power was channeled into safety features and control systems rather than everyone suddenly driving at 200 miles per hour. The technology diffused, society adapted, and the transformation was profound but gradual. That’s exactly how I expect quantum computing to enter the mainstream. There will be no clean “flip-the-switch” event where classical computing becomes obsolete. Instead, quantum processors will show up first as specialized accelerators inside hybrid stacks, attached to the workflows where they can add measurable value, and then broaden as hardware and software mature. We’re already seeing this pattern in the real world. At AisT in Japan, our Gemini-class system is installed alongside more than 2,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs in the ABCI-Q supercomputer. The model isn’t “quantum replaces classical.” It’s hybrid workflows, where some tasks are better suited to a qpuand others stay on GPUs and CPUs, with the system working as one. The hpccommunity understands this because they’ve lived through it: vector processors, massively parallel systems, GPUs, and aiaccelerators didn’t erase what came before. They layered onto the stack, expanded what was possible, and eventually became normal. For teams planning adoption: The practical playbook is the same. Start with a targeted pilot and a well-defined workflow. Build a repeatable hybrid loop. Let your team compound learning so that when capability crosses your threshold, you’re ready to operationalize, not just experiment. 6. Defense and National Security Jensen was direct about something that often goes unsaid in tech: he's comfortable with military applications of AI, and he believes defense-focused technology startups should be socially acceptable. He argued that democracies need strong defense capabilities, and that aiwill inevitably be part of that picture. I see this as an important application area. Quantum computing has significant national security implications beyond the cryptography concerns that get the most attention. Applications in logistics optimization, sensor networks, materials discovery for aerospace and defense, and secure communications all matter strategically. The United States, our allies, and democracies more broadly have a legitimate interest in leading this technology. I work at QuEra Computing Inc., a DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative Stage B selectee. We work with national laboratories and defense-adjacent partners. This isn't something we hide or feel conflicted about; It's part of what we do. I'd add one dimension to Jensen's framing: the quantum supply chain is genuinely global in ways that create both opportunities and challenges. Critical components (specialized lasers, vacuum systems, precision optics) often come from international suppliers. Building sovereign quantum capability isn't just about the quantum computer itself; it's about the entire stack of enabling technologies. This is why attention to domestic supply chain development is increasingly important. Technological leadership isn't just about what you can build. It's about ensuring you can continue to build it. For teams in defense-adjacent environments: The deciding factors are rarely about capability claims. They're operational: security controls, audit posture, access governance, and facility integration. Those requirements are why on-premises quantum is becoming a distinct category, especially for organizations operating under strict compliance and export-control regimes. What This Means If You're Evaluating Quantum in 2026 If Jensen's platform thesis resonates with you, here's the most practical way to apply it to quantum: Treat quantum like an emerging accelerator, not a distant moonshot. You are not betting on a single breakthrough moment. You are testing whether a hybrid workflow can deliver a measurable improvement on a real bottleneck, using tools your team can operate. Start with one workflow where you already feel pain and can define success. Pick a target problem where the physics or combinatorics are the limiting factor, like sampling, simulation, or a constrained optimization loop. Define a metric you would recognize on the classical side, like time-to-answer, solution quality, or the compute required to reach a given confidence level. Evaluate platforms by iteration speed and integration fit, not peak specs. Ask how quickly your team can run meaningful experiments, debug, and repeat. The key question is whether the platform supports a productive development loop, including emulation, workflow integration, and predictable operations. Use cloud to build intuition, then let security and operations drive deployment choices. For most teams, a short cloud-based evaluation is the lowest-friction way to develop internal capability and identify promising hybrid loops. If sovereignty, compliance, or ipconstraints apply to your target workloads, on-premises options become part of the roadmap. If they do not, cloud access may be sufficient. Assume diffusion and optimize for compounding learning. Quantum will become mainstream the same way GPUs did: through developer tooling, workflow integration, and the steady accumulation of real usage. The organizations that start compounding now will be positioned to operationalize when capability crosses their threshold. AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) The goal of ASTS is to create a ‘giant cellular base station floating in space.’ ​Key technology: By deploying a huge satellite antenna (approximately 693 sq ft) like BlueWalker 3 (BW3) into space, it can capture weak signals emitted by ordinary smartphones on the ground and re-radiate them. ​User Experience: Users will be able to use their existing smartphones for calls, texts, and data without a separate device, even in deserts, the middle of the ocean, and mountainous areas where telecommunication service providers do not provide service. ​Business model: Rather than users directly signing up for ASTS, existing carriers such as AT&T provide ASTS's network in a 'roaming' form. ​2. Starlink ​Starlink's goal is to provide high-speed Internet for use in fixed locations (homes, ships, airplanes) where terrestrial infrastructure is lacking. ​Core technology: Thousands of small satellites are densely spaced in low-Earth orbit (satellite swarm) to cover the entire Earth. ​User Experience: Users must install a dedicated antenna (Dishy). This antenna receives satellite signals and supplies internet through your Wi-Fi router. This is how smartphones connect to this Wi-Fi. ​New Business (Direct to Cell): Recently, Starlink also saw the potential of this market and partnered with T-Mobile to launch a direct smartphone connection service. However, as of 2025, the focus is on low-bandwidth services such as text messaging and emergency communication, and there is still a difference from ASTS's goal of '5G broadband'. ​Summary ​ASTS is a **pure-play** company in the 'D2D (Direct-to-Device)' market, and the company's fate depends on the success of this technology. ​Starlink is already a huge company with a huge revenue and infrastructure as a **'satellite isP'**, and D2D is one of their new expansion businesses.
